Prevention: Practise fruit protection by wrapping, bagging or sleeving individual or bunches of fruit with plastic paper bags to prevent adult fruit flies from laying eggs.
Chose a site far away (more than 1 km) from other crops that may be infested to prevent the flies crossing over.
Remove host plants like guava, chillies, citrus, avocado, melons, coffee, mangoes and wild fruits to reduce pest population.
Harvest early when crop is mature and green because over-ripened fruits attract fruit flies.
Use mulch and do not destroy long flowering weeds to attract natural enemies.
Protect natural enemies such as spiders, dragonflies, ladybird beetles and parasitic wasps through conservation of patches of natural vegetation such as lantana camara.
Monitoring: Look out for small, yellow flies, about 8 mm long, with bright green eyes and smoky bands across the wings.
Look out for prematurely dropped fruits and symptoms in the crop and disect them to look for white, cylindrical, and tapered maggots.
Set pheromone traps to detect fruit flies presence.
Consider direct control actions when one female fly is found per trap per week for both species.
Direct Control: Collect and destroy all infested fallen fruits by burying 40 cm deep, putting in a pool of water or putting on plastic containers and cover tightly twice a week for the entire season.
Set pheromone or protein bait traps at 2-4 traps per acre for fruit fly management.

Do not use chemicals with the same mode of action year after year as this can lead to resistance.
